scenes.title: Comprehensive Cache Coherence & Memory Consistency Mechanisms
scenes.subtitle: Dense multi-factor breakdown with long architectural terminology
narration_sentences: Multicore processors coordinate private caches using directory-based invalidation and snooping state transitions.
Each core tracks whether a sixty-four-byte cache line is Modified, Exclusive, Shared, or Invalid to prevent stale reads.
Store buffers hide write latency locally while memory fences enforce ordering across visible core boundaries.
False sharing occurs when independent threads modify different fields that happen to reside on the exact same cache line.
Hardware prefetchers detect sequential stride patterns early and issue speculative fills before demand misses stall execution.
Non-uniform memory access topologies add remote socket hop penalties when threads allocate pages far from their execution core.
Translation lookaside buffer shootdowns synchronize virtual-to-physical page table invalidations across every active hardware thread.
Structuring hot data per thread and padding contended counters prevents cross-core cache line bouncing under heavy parallel load.

items.label: ModifiedDirtyCacheLineOwnershipState
items.detail: Core holds the sole valid dirty copy; any remote read request forces a cache-to-cache write-back or memory flush before sharing.

items.label: ExclusiveVsSharedReadOnlyCoherenceTransitions
items.detail: Exclusive permits silent local upgrade to Modified on write, whereas Shared requires broadcasting an invalidation request across the interconnect.

items.label: StoreBufferAndStoreForwardingPipeline
items.detail: Pending stores queue locally so execution continues; memory barriers drain store buffers before subsequent loads become globally visible.

items.label: FalseSharingAcrossContiguousSixtyFourByteLines
items.detail: Two cores updating separate integers inside one 64-byte line repeatedly invalidate each other, collapsing multicore throughput.

items.label: HardwareStridePrefetchingAndBandwidthTradeoff
items.detail: Stream detectors fetch upcoming cache lines ahead of demand reads, though excessive speculation can pollute L2/L3 capacity.

items.label: NonUniformMemoryAccessInterconnectCoherenceProtocol
items.detail: Cross-socket memory requests traverse UPI or Infinity Fabric links, doubling latency compared to local memory controller channels.

items.label: TranslationLookasideBufferShootdownInvalidation
items.detail: Unmapping virtual pages triggers inter-processor interrupts so peer cores flush stale virtual-to-physical address translations.

items.label: CacheLineAlignedThreadLocalPartitioning
items.detail: Aligning per-worker accumulators on 64-byte boundaries isolates dirty writes and preserves near-linear multicore scalability.

scenes.title: End-to-End Virtual-to-Physical Cache Miss & Replacement Flow
scenes.subtitle: Eight-stage hardware lookup, translation, miss fill, and write-back pipeline
narration_sentences: First, the load unit issues a virtual address and queries the L1 data TLB alongside set index extraction.
Second, physical tag comparison checks all ways inside the indexed cache set in parallel.
Third, if no valid way matches, the miss status holding register allocates an outstanding fill entry.
Fourth, the L2 controller probes its larger inclusive or non-inclusive directory for the physical cache line.
Fifth, on an L2 and L3 miss, the memory controller issues a DRAM row-buffer activate and column read command.
Sixth, the replacement policy selects an LRU or pseudo-LRU victim way in L1 to make room for the incoming line.
Seventh, if the evicted victim line carries a set dirty bit, its contents enqueue into a write-back buffer to lower memory.
Eighth, the newly arrived 64-byte line fills the L1 way, marks valid, and wakes the stalled load instruction.

items.label: VirtualAddressAndTLBLookup
items.detail: Compute virtual page number and set index in parallel using VIPT geometry.

items.label: AssociativeTagComparison
items.detail: Compare physical tag bits against all 8 ways in the indexed L1 cache set.

items.label: MissStatusHoldingAllocation
items.detail: Record L1 miss in MSHR table so non-blocking loads merge into one fill request.

items.label: CoherenceDirectoryProbeL2L3
items.detail: Check L2, shared L3, and snoop filters for clean or Modified peer ownership.

items.label: DramMemoryControllerRead
items.detail: Schedule DRAM bank precharge, activate, and CAS read across memory channels.

items.label: VictimWaySelectionPolicy
items.detail: Pick least-recently-used replacement candidate way inside the target L1 set.

items.label: DirtyBitWriteBackFlush
items.detail: If victim dirty bit equals 1, push modified 64-byte line to write-back buffer.

items.label: CacheLineFillAndWakeup
items.detail: Install incoming line, update tag metadata, and forward requested word to core.

scenes.title: Seven Decades of Memory Hierarchy & Cache Milestones
scenes.subtitle: Dense timeline requiring horizontal split without overlapping cards
narration_sentences: In 1968, IBM System/360 Model 85 introduced the first commercial high-speed cache memory.
In 1974, early minicomputers experimented with small off-chip bipolar SRAM instruction buffers.
In 1984, Motorola 68020 integrated a 256-byte on-chip instruction cache directly on silicon.
In 1989, Intel 80486 unified an 8-kilobyte on-die L1 cache alongside pipelined integer execution.
In 1995, Pentium Pro placed dedicated backside L2 SRAM inside the processor package.
In 2001, server processors standardized multi-megabyte shared on-die L2 and L3 cache hierarchies.
In 2006, mainstream dual and quad-core CPUs relied on MESI coherence protocols across shared L3.
In 2022, 3D vertical cache stacking expanded L3 capacity past ninety-six megabytes per compute die.

items.label: IBM System/360 Model 85
items.detail: First commercial high-speed buffer cache hiding slower magnetic core memory latency.

items.label: BipolarSRAMInstructionBuffers
items.detail: Off-chip SRAM banks trimmed instruction fetch stalls on high-frequency minicomputers.

items.label: On-Die Instruction Cache
items.detail: Motorola 68020 placed a 256-byte instruction cache inside the microprocessor die.

items.label: Unified On-Chip L1 Cache
items.detail: Intel 80486 integrated an 8 KB unified L1 cache directly with the CPU pipeline.

items.label: Dedicated Backside L2 Bus
items.detail: Pentium Pro coupled full-speed L2 SRAM in a dual-cavity MCM package.

items.label: Multi-Megabyte Shared Tiers
items.detail: Enterprise processors moved large associative L2 and L3 banks onto the main die.

items.label: MulticoreCoherenceProtocols
items.detail: Shared L3 slices and MESI/MOESI snooping kept multi-core caches consistent.

items.label: 3DV-CacheStackedMemory
items.detail: Through-silicon vias bond extra SRAM tiles directly atop L3 for massive capacity.
